A 83-year-old male patient from a skilled nursing facility is admitted to the hospital due to a back ulcer
that has progressively enlarged over the past three weeks. He has been bedridden and hemiplegic
since a spinal cord injury one year ago, along with fecal and urinary incontinence. His medical history
includes hypertension managed with ramipril. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall, weighs 55 kg (121 lb), and
has a BMI of 18 kg/m². Vital signs are stable. Physical examination reveals 0/5 muscle strength in the
lower extremities and absent sensation below the umbilicus. A 5 × 3-cm full-thickness skin ulcer with
necrotic tissue and visible subcutaneous fat is present over the sacrum, with mild surrounding
erythema. Laboratory results are within normal limits. The patient is scheduled for surgical debridement
and fasciocutaneous flap placement. Which of the following factors is most likely to contribute to flap
failure in this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Decreased arterial supply to the wound bed (B) Impaired
sensory feedback (C) Inadequate flap tension (D) Poor nutritional status (E) Low serum albumin level
(F) Chronic pressure on the surgical site (G) Pretreatment of the wound bed with negative pressure
wound therapy (H) Presence of local bacterial colonization (I) Urinary and fecal contamination (J)
Remaining necrotic tissue in the wound bed
 A. Pretreatment of the wound bed with negative pressure wound therapy
B. Presence of local bacterial colonization
C. Inadequate flap tension
D. Impaired sensory feedback
E. Chronic pressure on the surgical site
F. Low serum albumin level

G. Remaining necrotic tissue in the wound bed
H. Decreased arterial supply to the wound bed
I. Poor nutritional status
J. Urinary and fecal contamination
